name: GiveDirectly cash transfers, wellbeing analysis
beneficiaries_note: Nothing in the model says where; the charity's main country of operation, the one its other models name most: Kenya.

missing_data.note: Measured: GiveDirectly counts its recipients, and the effect is from randomised trials of its own transfers.

summary: Sends cash transfers of about $1,000 to poor households in East Africa. The Happier Lives Institute's estimate of GiveDirectly's effect on wellbeing, from its meta-analysis of cash transfers' effects on life satisfaction and mental health, including spillovers to the household.

source.title: Cash transfers cost-effectiveness analysis
source.license: © Happier Lives Institute; no licence published

sections.title: Recipient, household and discounting
sections.explainer: charityevals' step, not HLI's. HLI's figure counts the recipient and the other members of the household together, and a year of better wellbeing the same whenever it comes. In our view the household's share is a side effect (the side-effects slider weighs it) and later years count less at the discount rate under Your values; the evaluator view counts both in full and sets the rate to 0, so HLI's figure is unchanged there.

rows.label: WELLBYs per $1,000
rows.explainer: HLI's current figure for GiveDirectly, which it uses as the benchmark for its other charities. HLI's earlier, more detailed model (2022) put it at 8.2 WELLBYs per $1,000. HLI's report explains the meta-analysis behind it; the summary sheet publishes only the result, and its December 2024 summary gives the recipient and household shares our steps below use.

rows.label: Recipient's share of the household's WELLBYs

source.title: HLI, GiveDirectly comprehensive summary (December 2024)
source.quote: a total effect over time of 2.10 WELLBYs on the recipient ... 7.12 WELLBYs for the other household members combined ... 9.22 WELLBYs for the whole household

rows.explainer: HLI's $1,000 transfer gives the recipient 2.10 WELLBYs and the four other household members 7.12 together (each 86% of the recipient's benefit), 9.22 in all: the recipient's share is 2.10 / 9.22 = 23%.

rows.label: WELLBYs per $1,000 for the other household members (spillover)
rows.explainer: The other household members' benefit, a spillover beyond the person given the cash: a side effect, weighed by the side-effects slider (docs/normalization.md 2.16).

rows.label: Discount rate on future wellbeing
rows.explainer: The shared discount rate (Your values). HLI doesn't discount, so the evaluator view pins it at 0.

rows.label: Years the benefits are spread over
rows.explainer: Our judgment from HLI's meta-analysis of cash transfers (McGuire, Kaiser and Bach-Mortensen, Nature Human Behaviour 2022): the effect on wellbeing fades linearly and is gone about seven years after the transfer; HLI's summary says only that the benefits dissipate linearly. Spread evenly over 7 years (4 to 12); an even spread discounts slightly more than a linear fade over the same years.

rows.label: Discount factor for benefits spread evenly over those years
rows.explainer: The present value of an equal benefit each year over the years above, starting with the transfer, as a share of the undiscounted total: 1 at a 0% rate.

rows.label: Staff pay as a share of program cost
rows.explainer: About 16% of GiveDirectly's costs are not transfers; we guess half of that is staff pay, as in our GiveDirectly model.

rows.label: Pay gap versus comparable jobs elsewhere
rows.explainer: Our judgment, as in our GiveDirectly model.

rows.label: Salary forgone by staff per dollar of cost (in-kind donation)
Share of the full cost paid in cash
rows.explainer: With credit by share of resources, staff's forgone pay counts as part of the cost, and staff get their share of the outcome. Off, this is 100%.

rows.label: WELLBYs per dollar
rows.explainer: With credit by share of resources, times the share of the full cost paid in cash (staff's forgone pay is the rest).
